Study Done Finds Counter-Intuitive Relationship Between Nations that Require more Vaccine Doses and Higher Infant Mortality Rates.

Given the recent Vaccine discussions here on voat, I found this study particularly interesting. I don't necessarily prescribe to the Anti-Vaxxer camp, but the correlation drawn here is worth taking note of and expanding upon further.

Efforts to reduce the relatively high US IMR have been elusive. Finding ways to lower preterm birth rates should be a high priority. However, preventing premature births is just a partial solution to reduce infant deaths. A closer inspection of correlations between vaccine doses, biochemical or synergistic toxicity, and IMRs, is essential. All nations—rich and poor, advanced and developing—have an obligation to determine whether their immunization schedules are achieving their desired goals.

Seeing how America not only specifies 26 vaccine doses for infants aged less than 1 year—the most in the world-- and spends more per capita on health care than any other country, they still rank behind 33 nations with concern of Infant mortality rates.... which elicits an important inquiry worthy of discussion and study: are some infant deaths associated with over-vaccination?

I'm married to an OB/Gyn who did a ton of work at Community Health Centers and Academic Hospitals so I want to throw out a couple theories why there may be a correlation.

In developed countries that have access to a lot of vaccines they typically have access to medicine. As much as people want to believe that the poor don't get any healthcare, they get quite a bit in the US. They just get a huge bill that they never pay. Most of my wife's patients at the Academic hospitals were of low socioeconomic status. Given the high level of care the doctors are able to see problems early and take measures to try and prevent an Inter-Uterine Fetal Death (IUFD). They may have issues that decrease quality of life and survivability. They will deliver babies at just the edge of viability and put them in the NICU when it's necessary to try and save the fetus and mother. These babies may end up fine but generally have poor outcomes including health complications and death. If the baby only lives a few days it gets counted as an infant mortality. Another common thing is that babies that have defects that are incompatible with life, meaning they have no chance of survival, mothers will want to carry to term. The baby lives an hour or less and gets counted as an infant death. Mostly they will do this because they don't believe in abortion even when there is a lethal abnormality. It was crazy how often this kind of thing happened. It wasn't always religious but the poor people she saw tended to do this. Another thing that ups these numbers is un-safe sleeping. Among the poor it is very common for them to co-sleep or provide an unsafe sleep setting, i.e. pillows, stuffed animals, or blankets. These deaths are usually listed as SIDS and just get tallied as infant deaths. These happens a lot due to poor education and just not understanding best practices. It's become very important for Peds and Obs to talk with their patients about safe sleep but these deaths are still extremely frequent.

Overall, all of these things contribute to higher infant death rates when compared to other countries that have better maternal education and different views on abortion. I'm willing to bet if they looked at just these (I'm sure there are other similar things that contribute too) they would see a correlation as well.

This study was published in a small fringe journal, and note the correction with the authors' affiliations. Neither has a background in medicine, epidemiology or immunology. There are also some problems in methodology such as intentionally only examining the US the those countries with better IMR than the US, instead of a range of countries of various IMR, and there was no attempt to control for confounding factors, like rates of premature birth (which is much higher in the US than in most European countries).
